 Solar generators can make your life a little easier on a good day or save you on a bad day. These powerful power packs offer huge battery capacity that can fuel large devices and even appliances in a pinch. They’re great in an emergency, but they’re also essential tailgating and camping equipment. We chose the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 as our best overall pick, but there are plenty of options to fit your specific neeeds.

 How we chose the best solar generators 
 As an avid outdoorsman, I’ve had the opportunity to test a wide range of outdoor gear, including mobile and off-grid electrification equipment like solar-powered generators, as well as inverter and dual-fuel generators. These became particularly essential when the pandemic forced my travels to become domestic rather than international, which prompted me to outfit a van for long-term road-tripping . 
 To bring my work along for the ride, I needed a constant portable power source to charge my laptop, a portable fridge, lighting, and a myriad of devices and tools … even electric bikes . As a result, I’ve tried all the leading portable power stations (and plenty that aren’t leading, too), so I know precisely what separates the best from the blah. I’ve written all about it (and other outdoor tech) for publications, including the Daily Beast , Thrillist , the Manual , Popular Science , and more. There were cases when my own opinion resulted in a tie, so I looked to reviews from actual customers to determine which solar generators delivered the most satisfaction to the most users. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 joined the list in November 2026 based on their published specs and how they stack up against the units we’ve tested; we haven’t put any of them through our own testing yet.
 When to buy a solar generator 
 If you’re thinking about dropping big money on a solar generator, consider shopping on big shopping holidays like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday. These are expensive devices, and they experience their largest discounts around those times. That said, they frequently sell below list price, even when it’s not a retail holiday, so click through to find out.
 The best solar generators: Reviews & Recommendations 
 The solar generators on this list span a wide range of budgets, from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand. They cover several uses, from camping to backup for your home . Only you know all the factors that make one of these the best solar generator for you , but we think that one of these will get the job done.

With a capacity of 2,073 watt-hours, it hits the sweet spot that will deliver on the needs of the vast majority of users. 
 At the same time, its compact dimensions make it easy to fit almost anywhere, though at 53.4 pounds it’s a two-hand lift. That makes it an easy pick for packing in a trunk while heading outdoors, storing in a closet for backup power, or simply having around for a convenient, mobile power source. 
 It also offers high output for its size. Its 2,600W running output was already hefty enough, and Bluetti’s Power Lifting mode can run resistive loads such as kettles and hair dryers at up to 3,900W. Its 1000W solar input capacity equips it for a large solar panel array, and its 1,800W wall input capacity will charge it from zero to full in about 1.4 hours, according to Bluetti. 
 While power station apps are notoriously glitchy, the Bluetti app is user-friendly and allows for remote monitoring and adjustment. Most users will find it has plenty of ports, including four AC ports, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a 120W car port, though there is no 30A or 50A RV plug.
 I’ve found that its squared-off design is ideal for fitting into a tight storage space or building into a small van conversion. The LiFePO4 battery has a lifespan of over 6,000 cycles, and the whole unit feels plenty durable. Indeed, I have knocked my test unit around more than a little. It seems no worse for wear.

Jackery rates it for 2,200W of continuous output and 4,400W surge, enough for a full-size fridge, a microwave or most corded tools. It refills from a wall outlet in about 1.7 hours, and Jackery says it keeps about 95 percent of its charge after 12 months in storage, so it can sit in a closet between outages.

 Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 keeps the original’s small footprint but moves to a LiFePO4 battery that Jackery rates for 4,000 cycles.
 Though it isn’t quite as impressive as our top picks for best overall and best high-capacity, the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 is compact, light, and a decent amount of power for its price. Less a mobile power station than an upscale power bank, the 8.16-pound Explorer 300 v2 handles device charging when you’re camping, on a job site, driving, or just need some power away from an outlet. Its 288Wh capacity isn’t huge, but it’s enough to keep phones, cameras and a laptop topped off, or run a small fan or light for a few hours. The 300W inverter (600W surge) won’t run a coffee maker, but it has a 100W USB-C port, and Jackery says a wall outlet refills it in about 76 minutes.
 We tested the original Explorer 300, the portable power station this one replaces, for several months, and it came in handy numerous times, especially during the winter when power outages abound. At one point, we had it powering two phones, a MacBook, and a small light. We haven’t tested the v2 yet, but it’s in the same size class with a longer-lived battery: Jackery rates its LiFePO4 cells for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity.
 Our original review unit got banged around in car trunks, duffel bags, and other less-than-luxurious accommodations with no issues. If you catch one of these on sale, get it and stick it in a cabinet. You’ll be extremely glad to have it around when the need arises.
 What to consider before buying the best solar generators 
 Over the past few years, solar generators have exploded onto the market. There are now dozens of different brands that largely look more or less the same at a glance. The fact is, there are only a few standouts among a sea of knockoffs. Here’s what to look for to ensure you’re getting a great one:
 How much power can it store?
 A portable solar generator comes in a wide range of sizes, but a generator’s size doesn’t automatically make it capable of storing a lot of power. In fact, most are disappointingly limited and unable to store much more juice than a portable charger .
 To properly check a generator’s storage, you must look at its capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh). One watt-hour is the equivalent of 1 watt flowing over the course of an hour. The best solar generators offer capacities of several hundred and sometimes several thousand watt-hours. That doesn’t mean, however, that it will provide power for several hundred or several thousand hours. Any generator will ultimately last a different amount of time, depending on what’s plugged into it.
 It’s easy to predict how long a generator will last when you use it to power one thing. For example, if you were to power a 100-watt bulb using a power station with a capacity of 500 watt-hours, it would stay lit for five continuous hours. Add a portable fridge with a 50W average draw, a phone charger drawing up to 18W, a 3W mini-fan, and runtime drops accordingly. The more capacity, the better.
 Charging capability
 No solar generator will hold a charge forever, so you want one capable of charging as quickly and easily as possible. This is where we put the “renewable” into “renewable energy.”
 All of the power stations included in this roundup can be charged by connecting them to solar panels (hence the designation “solar generators”). Still, you also want to look for the ability to charge via other sources like wall outlets and your vehicle’s 12-volt plug. This ensures that you can charge up whether you’re off-grid in the sun, plugged in while preparing at home, or using your dash socket on the go.
 You must also monitor a model’s charging input capacity, measured in watts (W). For example, a solar-powered generator with a max input of 100W can take in a continuous flow of up to 100 watts, which is about the minimum that you’ll reasonably want to look for. Most of the generators below have input capacities of at least a few hundred watts when charging via solar, so a few 50- to 200-watt solar panels will max them out.
 Output capability
 Solar generators need to keep the power coming in and going out. The best solar generators can simultaneously charge all your intended devices via whatever plugs are necessary.
 Any portable power station worth your money will have a high output capacity so you can charge many devices, even if they require a lot of juice. At a minimum, you’ll want a generator that can put out 300 watts at a time, though you’ll want at least 500 for larger tasks.
 The best solar generators should also offer a variety of output plugs, including AC outlets, USB-A, USB-C, and even 12-volt DC outlets like the one in your vehicle dash. This ensures you can charge several devices simultaneously regardless of their plug. The number of ports you’ll need will vary depending on how many devices you need to power, but it should have at least a couple of AC outlets and enough USB-C and USB-A ports, at suitable wattages, for your devices.
 Portability
 While portable battery sources have been around for a while now, over the past several decades, they’ve been pretty heavy, unwieldy things. One of the most exciting aspects of the latest generation of solar generators is that they’ve become much more physically compact. 
 Suppose you plan on taking a generator camping or working it into a van conversion where every square inch matters; well, size and weight become major considerations. All of the products we’ve recommended are about the size of one or two shoeboxes, three at the most. The lightest weighs about 7 pounds, while the heaviest standalone unit is about 84 pounds. Most fall somewhere between 30 and 60 pounds.
 If you’re using your generator as a more or less stationary source of backup power at home, portability isn’t a huge issue. Still, we generally recommend keeping weight and size in mind; you never know when you’ll need it for something other than a backup. (Plus, who wants to lug around something heavy and awkward if they don’t have to?) 
 Another consideration regarding portability involves the necessity for accessories, which can impact how easy it is to move and use your generator. Some generators, for example, require a lot of removable battery packs, which can be a hassle when you’re on the go or packing a vehicle. All of the picks on our list work on their own, though solar charging requires compatible panels and cables.
 Durability
 As with any product you expect to last, durability and all-around quality craftsmanship are essential. This is especially true if you plan on lugging your generator around on camping and road trips. Many subpar power stations are made from cheap components and flimsy plastic that doesn’t feel like it will hold up under the rigors of the road.
 Durability isn’t something you can determine by reading a spec sheet off the internet. You’ve actually got to take the generator out, use it a bunch, and see how it holds up. I’ve verified the durability of these recommendations via a combination of my own actual field tests and reviews culled from countless real product owners. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 are the exceptions; we haven’t tested them yet.
 Related: Best electric generators 
 FAQs 
 Q: What size solar generator should I get? It’s easy to underestimate how much capacity you need. 1,000 watt-hours might sound like a lot, but if you’re going to power a converted van with a portable fridge, lights, and occasional phone and laptop top-off, that 1,000 watt-hours will go faster than you expect. I used a setup like this and know from personal experience that you should always overestimate how much power you’ll need.
A generator with a capacity under 1,000Wh can keep electronics charged. A larger one with 1,000 to 1,500Wh should be the minimum for road trips where you’ll need it to last multiple days between full charges. For a house or worksite where you expect to use some serious energy, like a full-sized refrigerator or power tools, you’re going to want to start looking at the biggest possible power stations that can be daisy-chained to external batteries.
If you want to get precise, there is an equation :
1. Estimate how many hours you’ll need to power various devices. For example, if you want to power two light bulbs for two hours, you need two hours of operation.
2. Add up the total wattage necessary: the two bulbs are 60 watts each, so you need 120 watts.
3. Multiply these together to find the total watt-hours needed: 2 x 120 = 240Wh. Leave room for conversion losses and a reserve, and you’d want at least a 300Wh solar generator. 
That might sound like a lot for two lightbulbs, but remember that, in most situations, you won’t really be powering 60-watt light bulbs for hours on end. You’ll be charging phones and laptops for an hour here or there, cooling a fridge that kicks on and off every once in a while, using power tools in short bursts, and whatnot.
 Q: How many years will a solar generator last? Power stations are rated in charge cycles, not years. Jackery rates its v2 Explorers for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity, for example. How many years that adds up to depends on how often you drain and refill the battery, and on storing it within the manufacturer’s temperature range. The best-designed power stations are pretty sturdy, with few to no moving parts, so they should likely keep kicking for a long time, provided that you care for them properly. I’ve been pretty rough with a few of mine, and they show no signs of stopping. 
 Q: Can I run my house on solar power only? Yes and no. While it’s absolutely possible to power your house with solar power, you’re unlikely to do so with a portable solar generator unless you use several at once while limiting your power usage. High-capacity picks such as the Bluetti Apex 300 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus come closest when paired with extra batteries, but how long they last depends on what you run, how much solar you can add, and the weather. Running house circuits, rather than plugging appliances straight into the station, requires a transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician. Never backfeed power through a wall outlet. 
 Final thoughts on the best solar generators 
 Best overall: Bluetti Elite 200 V2 
 Still great: Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 
 Best high-capacity: EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus 
 Best for car camping: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 
 Best for off-grid living: Bluetti Apex 300 
 Best for home backup: Jackery HomePower 3000 
 Best for extreme cold: Bluetti Pioneer Na 
 Best budget: Jackery Explorer 300 v2 
 We’re living in a “golden age” for portable solar generators. When I was a kid, and my family was playing around with solar gear while camping in the ‘90s, the technology couldn’t charge many devices, so it wasn’t all that practical. 
 By contrast, the solar generators I’ve recommended here are incredibly useful. I’ve relied on them to power my work and day-to-day needs while road-tripping nationwide. They’re also great when the power goes out. When a windstorm cut the power at my house for a couple of days, I was still working, watching my stories, and keeping the lights on. 
 We haven’t even scratched the surface in terms of the potential offered by portable, reliable, renewable, relatively affordable power. What we can do now is already incredible. The potential for what may come next, though, is even more exciting.

 How we test solar generators
 Our product experts closely monitor the solar generator market, tracking popular models and the new innovations at trade shows like the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) and the National Hardware Show.
 For this guide, our experts conducted a detailed technical review of over 30 solar generators , then performed hands-on testing of the top dozen models, both in our Lab and in the homes of a dozen consumer testers over the course of several months. Our evaluations focused on the following:
 Philip Friedman 
 ✔️ Charge time and capacity 
 Verified claimed charging times using solar panels and AC wall outlets in our Lab.
 Tested claimed capacity by running electronic devices with corresponding energy loads (e.g., 1,500-watt heaters for large-capacity generators, laptops for small-capacity generators) in our Lab.
 Consumer testers measured solar charge times and capacity under real-world home conditions.
 Our engineers reviewed technical data to confirm shelf life (how long the charge lasts) and life cycle (number of recharges).
 ✔️ Usability 
 Checked total number of outlets to gauge how many devices can be charged simultaneously. 
 Assessed user-friendly features such as carrying handles, wheels, LED lights, and onboard storage.
 ✔️ Durability 
 Tested durability of both the generator and solar panels for long-term performance.

 What to look for when shopping for solar-powered generators
 Solar generators come in various shapes and sizes to meet different needs. Key factors to consider include:
 ✔️ Capacity: The more watts, the more power a generator can deliver, so consider your home’s power needs. Small generators have capacities around 250 watts, while larger ones offer 3,000 watts or more. Overloading a generator can damage it and connected electronics.
 Also consider run time: To power a 200-watt refrigerator for 10 hours, you'll need a 2,000-watt generator. For an eight-hour run of a 40-watt CPAP machine, a 500-watt generator is sufficient.
 ✔️ Solar panel compatibility: Solar panel capacity affects charging speed. Our experts recommend at least 100-watt solar panels, and daisy-chaining multiple panels can speed up charging. Generators can charge via wall outlets, but solar panels are the cheapest.
 ✔️ Battery type: There are three main battery types—lithium-ion, LiFePO4, and solid-state—each with pros and cons.
 Lithium-ion batteries are most common, offering safe, reliable power, and they have been the standard for solar generators for years.
 LiFePO4 batteries are the latest technology, providing longer life spans and faster charging, though they struggle in extremely cold temperatures.
 Solid-state batteries are emerging and rely on solid electrolytes rather than the liquid electrolyte solution found in lithium batteries. They offer higher capacities but tend to be bulkier and heavier.
 ✔️ Portability: Weight, which can range from 10 to over 100 pounds, often correlates with capacity. If you need to take your generator on the go, look for user-friendly features like wheels and telescoping handles for easier transport. Solar panels can also be heavy, so handles and carrying cases improve portability.
 How do I decide between a solar and a gas generator?
 Jillian Sollazzo 
 Gas backup generators were once the go-to for power outages, but our experts recommend considering solar-powered options. While gas generators are effective, they're noisy, fuel-hungry, and must be used outdoors to avoid harmful fumes. In contrast, solar-powered generators are emissions-free, safe for indoor use, and much quieter, ensuring they won't disrupt your household while keeping everything running. 
 When deciding between a solar generator and a gas generator, consider your power needs and budget. For lower power needs under 3,000 watts, solar generators are ideal, while gas generators work better for larger demands, especially 10,000 watts or more.
 If automatic backup power is essential, a standby gas generator is reliable and easier to install, although some solar options offer this with more complex setups. Solar generators are safer as they produce no emissions, making them suitable for indoor use, while gas generators can pose potential carbon monoxide risks. Read more in our guide to solar vs. gas generators . 
 Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
 How do solar-powered generators work?
 A solar generator is essentially a large rechargeable battery that powers electronic devices. The fastest way to charge it is to plug it into a wall outlet, like a phone or computer. However, you can also charge solar generators with solar panels, making them invaluable during extended power outages when plug-in charging isn’t an option.
 What size solar panels do I need?
 Large whole-house generators can integrate with rooftop solar panels , working like a battery backup system such as the Tesla Powerwall by storing energy until it's needed.
 You can also charge solar generators of all sizes with portable solar panels, which connect to the battery via a standard solar cable. These panels typically range from 100 to 400 watts and can be daisy-chained for faster charging.
 Depending on conditions, a solar generator may charge fully in as little as four hours, though it can take up to 10 hours or longer. Therefore, it's essential to plan ahead, especially when extreme weather is on the horizon.
 Advertisement - Continue Reading Below
 Why are solar-powered generators also called portable power stations?
 Since this is still an emerging category, the industry is still figuring some things out—including what to call this new type of generator. The market for solar-powered generators is also splitting into "portable" and "whole-house" categories, similar to how gas generators come in portable or standby models. By comparison, whole-house power stations, while heavy (more than 100 pounds), are technically portable because they can be moved, unlike standby generators. However, consumers are unlikely to haul one outside to charge via solar power.

As the director of the Home Improvement & Outdoor Lab at the Good Housekeeping Institute, DiClerico oversees solar generator testing with our engineers, product analysts, and consumer testers. He regularly attends trade shows to stay current on industry innovations and to speak on housing and home improvement topics.

 How to Spot a Fake Black Friday Power Station Deal 
 Power station discounts look enormous on paper. Five checks sort the real ones out in under a minute. 
 1 Ignore the “was” price
 The brand sets it, and it can stay inflated for months . Compare with the lowest price we have tracked instead.
 2 Compare price per kWh
 A “50% off” 2kWh unit can cost more per kWh than a “20% off” 3kWh one. On Sep 26, 1kWh-class units ranged from $390 to $731 per kWh .
 3 Price the station alone first
 Solar bundles carry the biggest headline discounts because the panel is priced high to begin with .
 4 Flash and member prices are short
 EcoFlow shows members-only prices and several brands run sales that last a few hours . Check on the day.
 5 Check it is the current model
 Clearance on a replaced model can be fine, but compare it with its successor at the same price. Our reviews flag replaced models.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 When do Black Friday power station deals start in 2026? Black Friday is on November 27, 2026 and Cyber Monday on November 30. Based on 2025, expect Jackery, EcoFlow, BLUETTI and Anker SOLIX to open early Black Friday sales in the first half of November, with the deepest prices from about November 20 through Cyber Monday and extensions into early December. Anker SOLIX opened its 2026 Early Access sale on November 10, through November 18.
 Is Black Friday the cheapest time to buy a portable power station? Usually, yes, but not by as much as the banners suggest. In 2025 the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 sold for $479 on jackery.com during Black Friday, while its regular price in September 2026 is $559. Brands also run flash sales all year: Anker SOLIX held 72-hour sales every few weeks in early 2026. Compare the price with the lowest price we have tracked, not with the list price.
 Do Black Friday power station prices last until Cyber Monday? Mostly. In 2025, Jackery and Anker SOLIX prices held through Cyber Monday, and some Anker prices dropped further after November 20. EcoFlow’s lowest prices were rotating 24 to 48 hour flash deals, and BLUETTI used 72-hour flash windows in 2024. If a flash price fits your budget, do not count on it coming back.
 What happens if the price drops after I buy? All four brands have advertised a 30-day price match or refund of the difference on their own store, with exclusions. EcoFlow excludes flash-sale and members-only prices. A purchase made in the first half of November is usually still within 30 days on Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Check the terms on the promotion page on the day you buy.
 Are the prices on this page up to date? Yes. Prices are read automatically from each brand’s US store several times a day, and each table shows when it was last checked. During flash sales a price can change within the hour, so the price in your cart on the brand store is the one that counts.
 What size power station should I buy on Black Friday? Match it to your devices, not to the discount. A 1kWh unit covers a CPAP for two to three nights or a full-size fridge for 6 to 8 hours. Around 2kWh runs a full-size fridge for 12 to 17 hours. For a full 24-hour outage, plan on 2,500Wh or more. Home backup with a well pump or 240V appliances needs 3kWh or more and enough output.  Price per kWh: the fastest way to spot a real deal
 A big "% off" badge tells you little. What you are buying is stored energy, so divide the price by the battery capacity in kWh. That one number lets you compare a $499 unit with a $3,049 unit on equal terms.
 Three things stand out this year:
 2 kWh units beat 1 kWh units. The Bluetti Elite 200 V2 ($434/kWh) and Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 ($465/kWh with ECO50) cost less per kWh than any 1 kWh model we stock.
 The 3.5 kWh class is the value leader. The Mango Power E at about $368/kWh is the cheapest way to get more than a day of essentials from one box.
 240V costs extra. The HomePower 3600 Pro Max (about $558/kWh with ECO100) and Apex 300 (about $614/kWh) cost more per kWh for their 240V output, and both were sold out on November 16; the Mango Power E 240V kit (about $354/kWh with ECO100) is the in-stock 240V option. You pay for split-phase output and big inverters, which only makes sense if you need to run a well pump or other 240V loads.
 Size it before you buy: the 3-minute math
 A deal on the wrong size is not a deal. Use this quick method, or run your list through our Solar Kit Calculator .
 Step 1: add up daily energy (kWh)
 A typical outage list: refrigerator 1.5 kWh + Wi-Fi router and modem 0.5 kWh + 10 LED bulbs for 5 hours 0.45 kWh + phones and a laptop 0.2 kWh = about 2.65 kWh per day .
 Step 2: divide by 0.85 for usable capacity
 Inverter losses and reserve mean you get about 85% of the rated battery. 2.65 ÷ 0.85 = 3.1 kWh of battery for 24 hours . That points to a 3.5 kWh class unit such as the Mango Power E or HomePower 3600 Pro Max. A 2 kWh unit covers the same list for about 15-16 hours, which is enough for an overnight outage.
 Step 3: check starting watts, not just running watts
 Motors draw 3-5 times their running power for a moment at start-up. A fridge that runs at 150 W can need 1,200 W to start; a 1 HP well pump that runs at about 1,200 W can need 3,500-4,500 W and usually 240V. If your list includes a well pump, filter for 120/240V units with 6,000 W or more.
 Step 4: plan the recharge
 Daily solar harvest ≈ panel watts × peak sun hours × 0.8. Two 200 W panels in 4 sun hours give about 1.3 kWh per day, roughly half of the essentials list above. Buying panels in a bundle during the sale usually costs less than adding them in spring.
 Safety note: to power hardwired circuits, use a transfer switch, a home power panel or an inlet box with an interlock, installed by a licensed electrician. Never backfeed your house through a dryer or wall outlet.

 How to Choose in 60 Seconds
 Just keep the fridge and lights alive? Elite 200 V2 — best value, done. Living in it full-time or on wheels? Elite 300 for the RV outlet, or DELTA 2 Max if you'll expand later. Carrying it weekly? Jackery 2000 v2. Running real appliances, tools, or a mini-split sometimes? DELTA Pro. Weekend cabin on a budget? Jackery 1000 v2 plus a panel.
 Not sure what size you need? Run your actual appliances through our tiny home solar generator guide first — oversizing is the most expensive mistake in this category, and every deal above will still be here this week. Powering a kit build too? See how these fit the full budget in Amazon tiny homes under $10,000 .
 Buy Before the Storm, Not During It
 Black Friday timing and storm season overlap for a reason — and it's the best reason on this page to buy now rather than wait. When an Oklahoma ice storm knocks power out, everyone suddenly wants a generator at the same time: prices spike, stock sells out, and fuel lines form. A solar generator bought on sale in November is already charged, already in your garage, and it recharges from the sun without a single trip to a gas station.
 What outage power actually looks like with these units: a 2kWh-class station (Elite 200 V2, Jackery 2000 v2, DELTA 2 Max) keeps a modern fridge running roughly a day, phones and laptops charged indefinitely, lights on, and a CPAP machine through the night. The DELTA Pro stretches that to whole-tiny-home backup for a day or more. None of them runs electric heat or all-day air conditioning — size for the essentials, not the whole house.
 The storm-ready checklist: (1) Keep the unit charged to 80–100% from November through February — LiFePO4 batteries hold a charge for months. (2) Store one solar panel where you can reach it, not buried behind winter gear — even weak winter sun adds meaningful charge. (3) Know your essentials' wattage before the outage, not during it — fridge, phones, lights, medical devices first. (4) If you rely on a well pump or electric heat, step up to the DELTA Pro class or keep a fuel generator as backup — solar alone won't cover those loads.
 That's the whole pitch: the Black Friday price is the excuse, but the ice storm is the reason. Buy it while it's cheap and in stock, not while the lights are out.
 ⚠️ The two honest warnings. (1) Panels are not included in any price above — budget another $150–$400 for 200–400W of panels if you're going off-grid. (2) A 2kWh box will not run electric heat or all-day air conditioning. Sellers' "powers your whole home" ads assume tiny loads; the fridge-hours in our guide are the numbers to trust.
 Price-Checking Promise
 Every price on this page was checked on October 22, 2026 against the model's current Amazon listing price as tracked by national deal roundups (Popular Science's power-station deal tracking and 9to5Toys' EcoFlow sale coverage), cross-checked with the brands' published specs. Black Friday pricing moves fast — sometimes daily — so always confirm the final price at checkout . We re-check this page every week through November 30, 2026 and update the date stamp at the top whenever a price moves. If you spot a price that's changed before we do, the checkout price is the real one.
 FAQ
 When do these deals end?
 Bluetti has announced its Black Friday pricing runs through December 3 . Amazon's prices can change or sell out at any time — last year the best 2kWh deals briefly dipped again on Black Friday itself, then rose for December.
 Will prices drop more on Black Friday itself?
 Maybe by a little. Historically, early-November prices on these brands land within about 5–10% of the Black Friday floor, and the most popular models risk selling out. If a price above fits your budget, the bird in hand is usually worth it.
 What size does a tiny home actually need?
 2kWh class for fridge + lights + devices (about 14–20 fridge-hours per charge). 3kWh+ if a mini-split, electric cooking, or a well pump joins the list. Our sizing guide walks the math appliance by appliance.
 Can these run a mini-split?
 A 9,000 BTU mini-split draws ~700–1,000W running. A 2kWh unit gives you roughly 2 hours of compressor time — good for cooling a loft to sleep, not all-day AC. The DELTA Pro is the realistic pick for AC duty.
 Amazon or the brand's store — which is cheaper?
 It flips weekly during the season. Brands add coupon codes and free-panel bundles at their own stores; Amazon counters with Prime prices. Check both — that's exactly what our weekly refresh does.

 What the numbers say for solar buyers
 Best value with plenty of solar headroom: BLUETTI Apex 200 and Elite 200 V2
 The Apex 200 ($1,099, $429/kWh) takes up to 3,000 W of solar, so its cap will never be the limit for a home array; about 670 W of panel rating refills it on a 4.5-sun-hour day by our math. Its solar setup is more involved than most (two input types), so read our Apex 200 solar input guide first. The Elite 200 V2 ($899, $434/kWh) has a 1,000 W cap and needs about 540 W of panels for a one-day refill. Note that in our kit comparison it needed its two panels wired in series , because the parallel current went over its limit ( series vs parallel ).
 Cheap per kWh, but solar-limited: DELTA 3 Max and DELTA 3 Ultra
 The DELTA 3 Max ($879) and DELTA 3 Ultra ($1,299) tie the best price per kWh, but their solar caps ( 500 W and 800 W ) are small for their batteries. Both need about 4.5–4.8 peak sun-hours at full input to refill from empty, so a typical fall day gets you close, and a short winter day doesn’t. That’s fine if you mostly recharge from the wall or a generator and use solar to top up.
 The 400 W cap problem: Explorer 2000 v2 and HomePower 1000 Plus v2
 The Explorer 2000 v2 has a 2,042 Wh battery but a 400 W solar cap, so it needs about 6 sun-hours at full input. If you plan to rely on solar during a long outage, a 2 kWh station with an 800 W or higher cap (Anker C2000 Gen 2, Elite 200 V2, HomePower 2000 Plus v2) refills about twice as fast for similar money. The HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is also capped at 400 W, but with a 1,024 Wh battery that still means about 3 sun-hours.
 Fast solar, but you pay for it: F3000, F3800 Plus, DELTA Pro 3, Apex 300
 These four accept 2,400–3,200 W of solar and can refill in about 1.4–1.9 sun-hours with a big enough array, but they cost $542–$683 per kWh . They make sense if you have room for a large array or plan a permanent backup setup. See our flagship comparison and the Black Friday panel prices for what that much solar costs.
 What about the owner’s setup?
 The site owner’s four Jackery SolarSaga 200W panels (800 W) peaked at 696 W on a sunny October 29 on an Explorer 2000 Plus ( owner-tested write-up ). An 800 W array like that fits every station above with an 800 W or higher cap. On a 400 W or 500 W station, a good chunk of it would go unused at midday. The Explorer 2000 Plus itself (1,400 W cap) no longer showed a standalone listing on Jackery’s store feed on Nov 12; its successor, the HomePower 2000 Plus v2, caps solar at 800 W ( v2 vs Explorer 2000 Plus ).
